That increased Abrahah's anger and rage, and he swore that he would certainly raid Banu Kinanah and certainly demolish the House.

Then when Abrahah resolved to march toward the House, he ordered the Habashan (the Abyssinian troops) to prepare and equip themselves, and he went out with the elephant. The Arabs heard of that, and they regarded it as grave and were horrified by it, and they saw that fighting him was an obligation upon them, when they heard that he intended to demolish the Ka'bah, the Sacred House of God. A man who was among the nobles and kings of Yemen, called Dhu Nafr, went out, and called his people and those among the rest of the Arabs who answered him, to fight Abrahah and to strive against him for the House of God, and against what he intended of its demolition and ruin. Those who answered him answered, and he confronted him and fought him, and he was defeated and his companions scattered, and Dhu Nafr was taken prisoner. When Abrahah wished to kill him, Dhu Nafr said: "O king, do not kill me, for perhaps my remaining with you will be better for you than my killing." So he spared him from death, and held him in bonds with himself. Abrahah was a forbearing man.

Then Abrahah proceeded on that course of his, aiming at what he had set out for, until, when he was in the land of Khath'am, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami confronted him, with the two Khath'am clans, Shahran and Nahis, and those with him from the Arab tribes. He fought him, and Abrahah defeated him and took him prisoner, and he was brought to him. When he resolved to kill him, Nufayl said to him: "O king, do not kill me, for I am your guide in the land of the Arabs, and these two hands of mine are yours over my clans, Shahran and Nahis, with hearing and obedience." So he pardoned him and released him, and he went out with him, guiding him on the road. When he passed by al-Ta'if, Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib went out to him with men of Thaqif, and said: "O king, we are only your slaves, listening to you and obeying you; there is no opposition from us to you, and this house of ours is not the house you seek" — meaning al-Lat — "you only seek the house that is in Mecca" — meaning the Ka'bah — "and we will send with you someone to guide you." So he overlooked them, and they sent with him Abu Righal. Abrahah set out, and Abu Righal was with him, until he brought him down at al-Mughammas. When he had brought him down there, Abu Righal died there, and the Arabs stoned his grave, and it is the grave which people stone at al-Mughammas.

When Abrahah alighted at al-Mughammas, he sent a man from the Abyssinians, called al-Aswad ibn Maqsud, with horses of his, until he reached Mecca, and he drove to him the property of the people of Mecca from Quraysh and others, and he seized two hundred camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, who at that time was the chief and lord of Quraysh. Quraysh, Kinanah, Hudhayl, and whoever was with them in the Sanctuary of the people resolved to fight him, then they realized they had no power against him, so they abandoned that. Abrahah sent Hunatah al-Himyari to Mecca and said to him: "Ask about the lord of this city and its nobleman, then say to him: The king says to you: I have not come to fight you; I have only come to demolish the House. If you do not stand in its way with war, I have no need for your blood. If he does not wish to fight me, then bring him to me."

When Hunatah entered Makkah, he asked about the leader and noblest of Quraysh, and was told: ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hashim ibn ʿAbd Manaf ibn Qusayy. So he came to him and told him what Abrahah had ordered. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said: "By God, we do not intend to fight him, nor do we have the strength for that. This is the Sacred House of God, and the house of His friend Abraham, peace be upon him—or as he said. If He protects it, it is His house and His sanctuary; and if He leaves it between Abrahah and it, by God, we have no one to defend it against him—or as he said." Hunatah said to him: "Then come with me to the king, for he has ordered me to bring you to him." So ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib set out with him, accompanied by some of his sons, until they reached the army. He asked about Dhu Nafar, who was a friend of his, and was directed to him. He came to him while he was in his confinement and said: "O Dhu Nafar, do you have any means of help regarding what has befallen us?" Dhu Nafar, who was his friend, replied: "What help can a man have who is a captive in the hand of a king, awaiting to be killed morning or evening! I have no help in anything that has befallen you, except that Unays, the driver of the elephant, is a friend of mine. I will send for him and charge him with you, and impress upon him the magnitude of your right, and ask him to seek permission for you to see the king, so you may speak to him about what you want, and he may intercede for you with him for good, if he is able to do so." He said: "That is enough for me." So Dhu Nafar sent to Unays, and he came, and Dhu Nafar said: "O Unays, ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib is the leader of Quraysh and the owner of the caravans of Makkah; he feeds people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain tops, and the king has taken from him two hundred camels. So seek permission for him to see him, and plead his cause with him as much as you can." He said: "I will do so."
Unays spoke to Abrahah, saying: "O King, this is the leader of Quraysh at your gate, seeking permission to see you, and he is the owner of the caravans of Makkah, who feeds people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain tops. So grant him permission to see you, that he may speak to you about his need, and be kind to him." He said: Abrahah granted him permission. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was an imposing, handsome, and large man. When Abrahah saw him, he was struck with awe of him and honored him, and disliked that the Abyssinians should see him sit beneath him, so Abrahah got down from his throne and sat on his carpet, and made him sit beside him on it. Then he said to his interpreter: "Ask him what his need of the king is." The interpreter said that to him, and ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said: "My need of the king is that he return to me my two hundred camels which he has taken from me." When he said that, Abrahah said to his interpreter: "Tell him: I was impressed by you when I saw you, but I lost interest in you when you spoke to me. Do you speak to me about two hundred camels that I have taken from you, and leave aside a house which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, which I have come to demolish, and not speak to me about it?" ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said to him: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." He said: "He will not prevent me." He said: "Then that is your affair; return my camels to me."
It was said by some scholars that Yamur ibn Nufathah ibn ʿAdi ibn al-Dil ibn Bakr ibn ʿAbd Manaf ibn Kinanah, who was then the leader of the Banu Kinanah, went with ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib to Abrahah when Hunatah had sent for him, as did Khuwaylid ibn Wathilah al-Hudhali, who was then the leader of Hudhayl. They offered Abrahah a third of the wealth of Tihamah on condition that he would turn back from them and not demolish the House, but he refused, and God knows best.
Abrahah had returned to ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib the camels that had been taken for him. When they left him, ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib went back to Quraysh and informed them of the news, and ordered them to leave Makkah and take refuge in the mountain peaks and the ravines, fearing for them the harm of the army. Then ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib stood, took hold of the ring of the door of the Kaʿbah, and with him stood a group of Quraysh, supplicating God and seeking His aid against Abrahah and his troops. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, while holding the ring of the Kaʿbah's door, said:
O Lord, I do not hope for them other than You; O Lord, protect from them Your sanctuary.
Surely the enemy of the House is he who is hostile to You; prevent them from ruining Your dwelling.
[[The narration 179 – its chain is weak, as its weakness was explained earlier: 137. This wording was transmitted by Ibn Kathir 1:50 without chain or attribution. Al-Suyuti 1:14 transmitted it in abridged form and attributed it to al-Tabari only.]]
And he also said:
O God, indeed a man defends his camp; so defend Your sanctuary.
Let not their cross and their stratagem prevail against Your stratagem tomorrow.
If You do so, then perhaps You will have a purpose that You have in mind.
And if You do so, it is a matter by which You complete Your deed.
[[The report 180 – its chain is very weak, despite our ignorance of the state of some of its narrators: Musa ibn Sahl al-Razi, Tabari's teacher: we have not determined which man he is; perhaps he is "Musa ibn Sahl ibn Qadim, also said Ibn Musa Abu ʿUmar al-Ramli, originally from Nasa". He is a teacher of al-Tabari recorded in al-Tahdhib 10:347, but he is not described as "al-Razi". In the manuscript it was written: "Sahl ibn Musa"! We have not found this biography either, and we think it is a scribal error. And Yahya ibn ʿAwf: we have never found a biography of anyone by this name in the references available to us. As for the defect of the chain, it is "al-Furat ibn al-Sa'ib al-Jazari", who is very weak. Al-Bukhari said in al-Kabir 4/1/130: "They abandoned him, he is munkar al-hadith", and the imams likewise said of him. Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin (folio 187): he was one who narrated fabrications from the trustworthy, and brought mu'dal reports from the reliable; it is not permissible to argue with him, nor to narrate from him, nor to write his hadith except as a matter of testing. As for Maymun ibn Mihran, he is a well-known trustworthy Successor, a jurist and authority.
This report was transmitted by Ibn Kathir 1:50 without identification, with the wording "It was said: it is Islam". Al-Suyuti 1:15 transmitted it attributed to Ibn Jurayj only, with a typographical error in it: "Ibn Jurayj"!]]
And he also said:
Whenever a transgressor came with an evil intent, we hoped that it would be so for us.
So they turned back, obtaining nothing but disgrace, and the calamity destroyed them there.
I have never heard of men more vile than those who sought glory and violated Your sanctuary.
They dragged the hosts of their lands and the elephant, so that they might take your women captive.
[[The report 181 – Ibn al-Hanafiyyah: he is Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, and al-Hanafiyyah was his mother, Khawlah bint Jaʿfar from the Banu Hanifah; he became known by her ascription. The chain to him is weak: Muhammad ibn Rabiʿah al-Kilabi al-Ruʾasi: trustworthy, one of the teachers of Ahmad and Ibn Maʿin. Ismaʿil al-Azraq: he is Ismaʿil ibn Salman, and he is weak; Ibn Maʿin said: "his hadith is nothing", and Ibn Numayr and al-Nasa'i said: "abandoned"; Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin (p. 78, no. 35): "he alone narrates strange reports which he transmits from the well-known". Abu ʿUmar al-Bazzar: he is Dinar ibn ʿUmar al-Asadi al-Kufi, the blind, and he is trustworthy. The report was mentioned by Ibn Kathir 1:51 without attribution or chain.]]
Then ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib released the ring of the Kaʿbah's door, and he and those with him from Quraysh went up to the mountain peaks, where they took refuge, waiting to see what Abrahah would do to Makkah when he entered it. When Abrahah rose in the morning, he prepared to enter Makkah, readied his elephant, and arrayed his army; the elephant's name was Mahmud, and Abrahah was resolved to demolish the House and then return to Yemen. When they turned the elephant, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami came up, stood by its side, took hold of its ear and said: "Kneel down, Mahmud, and return safely whence you came, for you are in the sacred land of God." Then he released its ear, and the elephant knelt down. Nufayl ibn Habib ran off and climbed up the mountain. They struck the elephant to make it stand, but it refused; they struck it on the head with the tabarzin to make it stand, but it refused. They then thrust their hooks into its groin and goaded it to make it stand, but it refused. They turned it back toward Yemen, and it got up and trotted; they turned it toward Syria, and it did the same; they turned it toward the east, and it did the same; they turned it toward Makkah, and it knelt. God sent upon them birds from the sea, like swallows, each bird carrying three stones: a stone in its beak and two in its feet, like chickpeas and lentils. It did not strike any of them without their perishing, though not all of them were struck. They fled in haste along the road by which they had come, asking about Nufayl ibn Habib to guide them to the road to Yemen. Then Nufayl ibn Habib, when he saw what God had sent down upon them of His vengeance, said:
Where is the escape, when the Seeking God is the Pursuer? The one with the cleft lip is defeated, not the victor.
[[The report 182 – this is from the tafsir of al-Suddi, and its chain has been explained earlier: 168. Ibn Kathir 1:50 and al-Suyuti 1:15 transmitted it.]]
They fled, falling by every road and perishing at every watering place. Abrahah was struck in his body, and they carried him with them; his fingers fell off one by one, and each time a finger fell, it was followed by a discharge that dripped pus and blood, until they brought him to Sanaa, and he was like a young bird. He did not die until his chest split open from his heart, so they claim.
⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Yaʿqub ibn ʿUtbah ibn al-Mughirah ibn al-Akhnas, that he related that the first measles and smallpox were seen in the land of the Arabs that year, and that the first thing seen there was the bitter trees: the harmal, the colocynth, and the ʿushr, that year.
⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning his words: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ Abrahah al-Ashram came one day from Abyssinia, with those who were counted among the people of Yemen, to the House of God to demolish it, on account of a church they had which the Arabs had destroyed in the land of Yemen. They came with their elephant until, when they were at al-Saffah, it knelt down; whenever they turned it toward the House of God, it lay its neck on the ground, and whenever they turned it toward their own land, it went off at a trot. Until, when they were at Nakhlah al-Yamaniyyah, God sent upon them birds, white, in flocks. The ababil means many. With each bird were three stones: two in its feet and one in its beak. They kept striking them with them until God, mighty and majestic, made them like eaten chaff. He said: Abu Yaksum, who is Abrahah, escaped, and whenever he arrived in a land some of his flesh would fall off, until he reached his people, informed them of the news, and then died.
* *
As for His words: ﴿so He made them like eaten chaff﴾
That is, may He be exalted and remembered: God made the companions of the elephant like a crop that animals ate and then voided, so it dried up and its parts scattered. He likened the cutting apart of their limbs and the scattering of their body parts by the punishment that befell them to the scattering of the parts of the dung that results from eating the crop.
Some have said: al-ʿaṣf is the outer husk that surrounds the grain of wheat, like its covering.
Those who said that it refers to the leaves of the crop:
⁕ Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words: ﴿like eaten chaff﴾: he said: the leaves of wheat.
⁕ Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Mamar, from Qatadah: ﴿like eaten chaff﴾ he said: it is straw.
⁕ It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Muʿadh say: ʿUbayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say concerning His words ﴿like eaten chaff﴾: like eaten crops.
⁕ Muhammad ibn ʿAmarah al-Asadi narrated to me, saying: Zurayq ibn Marzuq narrated to us, saying: Hubayrah narrated to us, from Salamah ibn Nubayt, from al-Dahhak, concerning His words ﴿like eaten chaff﴾: he said: it is the hubur in Nabataean, and in another report: the maqhur (crushed).
⁕ Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words: ﴿So He made them like eaten chaff﴾: he said: the leaves of the crop and the leaves of herbs, when the beasts eat them and then void them, so they become dung.
Those who said that it refers to the husk of the grain:
⁕ Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿like eaten chaff﴾ he said: the wheat is eaten and its chaff is thrown away by the wind; al-ʿaṣf is what is above the wheat: it is the husk of the wheat.
Others said in this regard:
⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Sinan, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit: ﴿like eaten chaff﴾ he said: like food that has been eaten.
End of the tafsir of Surah al-Fil.

The interpretation of His words, exalted be His names: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plot go astray? And He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and He made them like eaten-up stalks.﴾

He, may His mention be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Have you not looked, O Muhammad, with the eye of your heart, so that you see by it ﴿how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant﴾, those who came from Yemen intending to destroy the Ka'bah, from Abyssinia, whose leader was Abrahah al-Habashi, the one with the cut nose, ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾

That is: Did He not make the effort of the Abyssinians, the companions of the elephant, in destroying the Ka'bah, ﴿go astray﴾, meaning: go astray from what they wanted and attempted of its destruction.

* *

As for His words: ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾

He, may His mention be exalted, says: And your Lord sent against them birds scattered, following one another from various directions. The word ﴿ababil﴾ (flocks) is a plural with no singular, like ash-shamatit and al-'abadid and the like. Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna claimed that he had not seen anyone assign a singular to it. Al-Farra' said: I have not heard from the Arabs anything regarding its singular. He said: Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi, who was trustworthy, claimed that he had heard that its singular is ﴿ibalah﴾ (إبالة). Al-Kisa'i used to say: I heard the grammarians say: ﴿ibul﴾ (إبول), like ﴿'ujul﴾ (عجول). He said: And I have heard some grammarians say: its singular is ﴿abil﴾ (أبيل).

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said something similar to what we have said about ﴿ababil﴾.

Those who said that:

• Sawwar ibn 'Abd Allah related to us, he said: Yahya ibn Sa'id related to us, he said: Hammad ibn Salamah related to us, from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, from Zirr, from 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: groups.

• Ibn Bashshar related to us, he said: Yahya and 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, both said: Hammad ibn Salamah related to us, from 'Asim, from Zirr, from 'Abd Allah, he said: the groups (al-firaq).

• 'Ali related to me, he said: Abu Salih related to us, he said: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: they follow one another.

• Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, he said: my father related to me, he said: my paternal uncle related to me, he said: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾, he said: they are those that follow one another.

• Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, he said: 'Abd al-A'la related to me, he said: Dawud related to us, from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal, that he said regarding ﴿birds in flocks﴾: they are herds (al-aqatee'), like camels gathered in groups (al-ibil al-mu'abbalah).

• Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Ya'qub al-Qummi related to us, from Ja'far, from Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza, ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: scattered.

• Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Waki' related to us, he said: al-Fadl related to us, from al-Hasan, ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: the many.

• Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Waki' related to us, from Isra'il, from Jabir, from Ibn Sabit, from Abu Salamah, the two said: ﴿al-ababil﴾ means the troops (al-zumar).

• Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, he said: Abu 'Asim related to us, he said: 'Isa related to us, and al-Harith related to me, he said: al-Hasan related to us, he said: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of God ﴿ababil﴾, he said: they are scattered, following one another, gathered together.

• Bishr related to us, he said: Yazid related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, he said: ﴿ababil﴾ means the many.

• Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, he said: ﴿ababil﴾ means the many.

• It has been related to me from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd related to us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾: he says: successive, one after another.

• Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾: ﴿ababil﴾ means the varied, coming from here and coming from there; they came to them from every place.

It has been mentioned that they were birds brought out from the sea. Some of them said: they came from the direction of the sea.

Then they differed regarding their description. Some of them said: they were white.

Others said: they were black.

Others said: they were green, with beaks like the beaks of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

• Ya'qub related to me, he said: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: Ibn 'Abbas said: they were birds, and they were birds with beaks like the beaks of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

• al-Hasan ibn Khalaf al-Wasiti related to me, he said: Waki' and Rawh ibn 'Ubadah related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from Ibn 'Abbas, the like of it.

• Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Waki' related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Ibn 'Abbas, something similar.

• Ya'qub related to us, he said: Hushaym related to us, he said: Husayn informed us, from 'Ikrimah, regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: they were birds that came out green, came out of the sea, with heads like the heads of beasts of prey.

• Ibn Bashshar related to us, he said: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, he said: Sufyan related to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: they are black birds of the sea, with stones in their beaks and talons.

• Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr: ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: black, of the sea, with stones in their talons and beaks.

• He said: Mihran related to us, from Kharijah, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: they had beaks like the beaks of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

• Yahya ibn Talhah al-Yarbu'i related to us, he said: Fudayl ibn 'Iyad related to us, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: green birds with yellow beaks, which moved among them.

• Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Waki' related to us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, he said: black birds carrying stones in their talons and beaks.

* *

As for His words: ﴿striking them with stones of hard clay﴾

He, may His mention be exalted, says: these birds, the ﴿ababil﴾ which God sent against the companions of the elephant, strike them with stones of ﴿sijjil﴾ (hard clay).

We have explained the meaning of ﴿sijjil﴾ in another place, but we will mention here some of what has been said about it, from the sayings of those whom we did not mention in that place.

Those who said that:

• Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from al-Suddi, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿stones of sijjil﴾, he said: clay in stones.

• al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Dhari' related to me, he said: Yazid ibn Zurayi' related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿striking them with stones of sijjil﴾, he said: of clay.

• Ibn Bashshar related to us, he said: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, he said: Sufyan related to us, from al-Suddi, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿stones of sijjil﴾, he said: sank wa-kul (Persian: stone and clay).

• al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Dhari' related to me, he said: Yazid ibn Zurayi' related to us, from 'Imarah ibn Abi Hafsah, from 'Ikrimah, regarding His words ﴿striking them with stones of sijjil﴾, he said: of clay.

• Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far related to us, he said: Shu'bah related to us, from Sharqi, he said: I heard 'Ikrimah say: ﴿striking them with stones of sijjil﴾, he said: sank wa-kul.

• Ya'qub related to me, he said: Hushaym related to us, he said: Husayn informed us, from 'Ikrimah, he said: They were striking them with stones, with which the smallpox (al-judari) came out upon whoever was struck. He said: That was the first day in which smallpox was seen; he said: it had not been seen before that day, nor after it.

• Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from Musa ibn Abi 'A'ishah, he said: Abu al-Kunud mentioned: smaller than a chickpea (al-himmasah) and larger than a lentil (al-'adasah).

• Ibn Bashshar related to us, he said: Abu Ahmad related to us, he said: Sufyan related to us, from Musa ibn Abi 'A'ishah, he said: the stones with which they were struck were larger than a lentil and smaller than a chickpea.

• He said: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri related to us, he said: Isra'il related to us, from Musa ibn Abi 'A'ishah, from 'Imran, the like of it.

• Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Waki' related to us, from Sufyan, from al-Suddi, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: sijjil in Persian: sank wa-kul, stone and clay.

• Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Waki' related to us, from Isra'il, from Jabir ibn Sabit, he said: it is in the foreign tongue: sank wa-kul.

• Bishr related to us, he said: Yazid related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, he said: With every bird were three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak, and it began striking them with them.

• Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿stones of sijjil﴾, he said: it is of clay.

• Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, he said: They were white birds that came out from the direction of the sea; with every bird were three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak, and it did not strike anything without crushing it.

• Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: 'Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Ya'qub informed us that his father informed him that it had reached him that the birds which struck with stones were carrying them in their mouths, and when they threw them, the skin blistered from them.

Others said: the meaning of that is: they strike them with stones from the lowest heaven.

Those who said that:

• Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿striking them with stones of sijjil﴾, he said: the lowest heaven, and he said: the lowest heaven is named sijjil, and it is the one from which God, may He be exalted and mighty, sent down (punishment) upon the people of Lut.

He said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: 'Amr ibn al-Harith informed us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal, that it had reached him that the birds which struck with stones were birds that come out of the sea, and that sijjil is the lowest heaven. And this saying that Ibn Zayd stated, we do not know any soundness for it in a report or in reason or in language, and the names of things are only known through a language in common use, or a report from God, may His mention be exalted.

The cause for which the punishment of God, may He be exalted, fell upon the companions of the elephant was the march of Abrahah al-Habashi with his army, with the elephant, toward the Sacred House of God to destroy it.

What prompted him to that was what:

• Ibn Humayd related it to us, he said: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us, he said: Ibn Ishaq related to us, that Abrahah built a church in San'a', and he was a Christian, and he named it al-Qulays; none like it had been seen in its time anywhere on earth. And he wrote to the Negus, king of Abyssinia: "Verily I have built for you, O king, a church, the like of which has not been built for any king before you, and I will not stop until I divert to it the pilgrims of the Arabs." [[Report 178 – this is a mawquf report on Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and its chain is sound: Mahmud ibn Khidash, with a kasra on the kha' and a fatha on the dal and a shin at the end, al-Talaqani: a trustworthy man of truthfulness, died on Wednesday, 14 Sha'ban 250, as in al-Tarikh al-Saghir of al-Bukhari: 247. Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Ru'asi: trustworthy, firm, intelligent; Ahmad and other memorizers related from him. Al-Hasan and 'Ali, the two sons of Salih ibn Salih ibn Hayy: both trustworthy, and they were twin brothers. Whoever spoke about al-Hasan spoke without proof, and we have authenticated him in al-Musnad: 2403, and his brother in it: 220. And 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Aqil ibn Abi Talib, and his mother Zaynab al-Sughra bint 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: a trustworthy Successor (tabi'i), and there is no proof for whoever spoke against him.

The report was transmitted by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:258–259, through the path of Abu Nu'aym from al-Hasan ibn Salih alone, with this chain. And he said: "This is a hadith with a sound chain, and the two (Bukhari and Muslim) did not narrate it." And al-Dhahabi agreed with him. And Ibn Kathir mentioned it, 1:50, and al-Suyuti 1:15, and al-Shawkani 1:13.]] When the Arabs spoke of Abrahah's letter to the Negus, a man from the Nasa'ah, one of Banu Faqim and then one of Banu Malik, became angry, so he went out until he came to al-Qulays, sat in it, then went out and joined his land. Abrahah was informed of that, and said: "Who did this?" It was said: "A man from the people of this House, which the Arabs make pilgrimage to in Mecca, who heard your words: 'I will divert to it the pilgrims of the Arabs,' so he became angry, and came and sat in it," meaning that it was not worthy of that. At that, Abrahah became furious, and swore that he would march upon the House and demolish it.

With Abrahah were men of the Arabs who had come to him seeking his favour, among them Muhammad ibn Khuza'i ibn Hizabah al-Dhakwani, then al-Sulami, along with a group of his people, and with him was a brother of his called Qays ibn Khuza'i. While they were with him, a servant of Abrahah came upon them, so he sent them his food, and he used to eat the testicles (al-khusa). When the people brought his food, they said: "By God, if we eat this, the Arabs will never cease to revile us with it as long as we live." So Muhammad ibn Khuza'i stood up, went to Abrahah and said: "O king, this is a day of festival for us, and we eat in it only the cheek-meat and the hands," and Abrahah said to him: "We will send to you whatever you wish, for I honoured you with my food, because of your standing with me."

Then Abrahah crowned Muhammad ibn Khuza'i and appointed him over Mudar, and ordered him to go among the people, calling them to pilgrimage to al-Qulayyis, his church which he built. Muhammad ibn Khuza'i set out until, when he alighted in some land of Banu Kinanah, and the people of Tihamah had learned of his affair and what he had come for, they sent to him a man from Hudhayl called 'Urwah ibn Hiyad al-Mula'i, who shot him with an arrow and killed him. Qays ibn Khuza'i, Muhammad's brother, was with him, and he fled when his brother was killed, and joined Abrahah and informed him of the killing. That increased Abrahah's anger and rage, and he swore that he would certainly raid Banu Kinanah and certainly demolish the House.

Then when Abrahah resolved to march toward the House, he ordered the Habashan (the Abyssinian troops) to prepare and equip themselves, and he went out with the elephant. The Arabs heard of that, and they regarded it as grave and were horrified by it, and they saw that fighting him was an obligation upon them, when they heard that he intended to demolish the Ka'bah, the Sacred House of God. A man who was among the nobles and kings of Yemen, called Dhu Nafr, went out, and called his people and those among the rest of the Arabs who answered him, to fight Abrahah and to strive against him for the House of God, and against what he intended of its demolition and ruin. Those who answered him answered, and he confronted him and fought him, and he was defeated and his companions scattered, and Dhu Nafr was taken prisoner. When Abrahah wished to kill him, Dhu Nafr said: "O king, do not kill me, for perhaps my remaining with you will be better for you than my killing." So he spared him from death, and held him in bonds with himself. Abrahah was a forbearing man.

Then Abrahah proceeded on that course of his, aiming at what he had set out for, until, when he was in the land of Khath'am, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami confronted him, with the two Khath'am clans, Shahran and Nahis, and those with him from the Arab tribes. He fought him, and Abrahah defeated him and took him prisoner, and he was brought to him. When he resolved to kill him, Nufayl said to him: "O king, do not kill me, for I am your guide in the land of the Arabs, and these two hands of mine are yours over my clans, Shahran and Nahis, with hearing and obedience." So he pardoned him and released him, and he went out with him, guiding him on the road. When he passed by al-Ta'if, Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib went out to him with men of Thaqif, and said: "O king, we are only your slaves, listening to you and obeying you; there is no opposition from us to you, and this house of ours is not the house you seek" — meaning al-Lat — "you only seek the house that is in Mecca" — meaning the Ka'bah — "and we will send with you someone to guide you." So he overlooked them, and they sent with him Abu Righal. Abrahah set out, and Abu Righal was with him, until he brought him down at al-Mughammas. When he had brought him down there, Abu Righal died there, and the Arabs stoned his grave, and it is the grave which people stone at al-Mughammas.

When Abrahah alighted at al-Mughammas, he sent a man from the Abyssinians, called al-Aswad ibn Maqsud, with horses of his, until he reached Mecca, and he drove to him the property of the people of Mecca from Quraysh and others, and he seized two hundred camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, who at that time was the chief and lord of Quraysh. Quraysh, Kinanah, Hudhayl, and whoever was with them in the Sanctuary of the people resolved to fight him, then they realized they had no power against him, so they abandoned that. Abrahah sent Hunatah al-Himyari to Mecca and said to him: "Ask about the lord of this city and its nobleman, then say to him: The king says to you: I have not come to fight you; I have only come to demolish the House. If you do not stand in its way with war, I have no need for your blood. If he does not wish to fight me, then bring him to me."

When Hunatah entered Makkah, he asked about the leader and noblest of Quraysh, and was told: ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hashim ibn ʿAbd Manaf ibn Qusayy. So he came to him and told him what Abrahah had ordered. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said: "By God, we do not intend to fight him, nor do we have the strength for that. This is the Sacred House of God, and the house of His friend Abraham, peace be upon him—or as he said. If He protects it, it is His house and His sanctuary; and if He leaves it between Abrahah and it, by God, we have no one to defend it against him—or as he said." Hunatah said to him: "Then come with me to the king, for he has ordered me to bring you to him." So ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib set out with him, accompanied by some of his sons, until they reached the army. He asked about Dhu Nafar, who was a friend of his, and was directed to him. He came to him while he was in his confinement and said: "O Dhu Nafar, do you have any means of help regarding what has befallen us?" Dhu Nafar, who was his friend, replied: "What help can a man have who is a captive in the hand of a king, awaiting to be killed morning or evening! I have no help in anything that has befallen you, except that Unays, the driver of the elephant, is a friend of mine. I will send for him and charge him with you, and impress upon him the magnitude of your right, and ask him to seek permission for you to see the king, so you may speak to him about what you want, and he may intercede for you with him for good, if he is able to do so." He said: "That is enough for me." So Dhu Nafar sent to Unays, and he came, and Dhu Nafar said: "O Unays, ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib is the leader of Quraysh and the owner of the caravans of Makkah; he feeds people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain tops, and the king has taken from him two hundred camels. So seek permission for him to see him, and plead his cause with him as much as you can." He said: "I will do so."
Unays spoke to Abrahah, saying: "O King, this is the leader of Quraysh at your gate, seeking permission to see you, and he is the owner of the caravans of Makkah, who feeds people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain tops. So grant him permission to see you, that he may speak to you about his need, and be kind to him." He said: Abrahah granted him permission. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was an imposing, handsome, and large man. When Abrahah saw him, he was struck with awe of him and honored him, and disliked that the Abyssinians should see him sit beneath him, so Abrahah got down from his throne and sat on his carpet, and made him sit beside him on it. Then he said to his interpreter: "Ask him what his need of the king is." The interpreter said that to him, and ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said: "My need of the king is that he return to me my two hundred camels which he has taken from me." When he said that, Abrahah said to his interpreter: "Tell him: I was impressed by you when I saw you, but I lost interest in you when you spoke to me. Do you speak to me about two hundred camels that I have taken from you, and leave aside a house which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, which I have come to demolish, and not speak to me about it?" ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said to him: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." He said: "He will not prevent me." He said: "Then that is your affair; return my camels to me."
It was said by some scholars that Yamur ibn Nufathah ibn ʿAdi ibn al-Dil ibn Bakr ibn ʿAbd Manaf ibn Kinanah, who was then the leader of the Banu Kinanah, went with ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib to Abrahah when Hunatah had sent for him, as did Khuwaylid ibn Wathilah al-Hudhali, who was then the leader of Hudhayl. They offered Abrahah a third of the wealth of Tihamah on condition that he would turn back from them and not demolish the House, but he refused, and God knows best.
Abrahah had returned to ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib the camels that had been taken for him. When they left him, ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib went back to Quraysh and informed them of the news, and ordered them to leave Makkah and take refuge in the mountain peaks and the ravines, fearing for them the harm of the army. Then ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib stood, took hold of the ring of the door of the Kaʿbah, and with him stood a group of Quraysh, supplicating God and seeking His aid against Abrahah and his troops. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, while holding the ring of the Kaʿbah's door, said:
O Lord, I do not hope for them other than You; O Lord, protect from them Your sanctuary.
Surely the enemy of the House is he who is hostile to You; prevent them from ruining Your dwelling.
[[The narration 179 – its chain is weak, as its weakness was explained earlier: 137. This wording was transmitted by Ibn Kathir 1:50 without chain or attribution. Al-Suyuti 1:14 transmitted it in abridged form and attributed it to al-Tabari only.]]
And he also said:
O God, indeed a man defends his camp; so defend Your sanctuary.
Let not their cross and their stratagem prevail against Your stratagem tomorrow.
If You do so, then perhaps You will have a purpose that You have in mind.
And if You do so, it is a matter by which You complete Your deed.
[[The report 180 – its chain is very weak, despite our ignorance of the state of some of its narrators: Musa ibn Sahl al-Razi, Tabari's teacher: we have not determined which man he is; perhaps he is "Musa ibn Sahl ibn Qadim, also said Ibn Musa Abu ʿUmar al-Ramli, originally from Nasa". He is a teacher of al-Tabari recorded in al-Tahdhib 10:347, but he is not described as "al-Razi". In the manuscript it was written: "Sahl ibn Musa"! We have not found this biography either, and we think it is a scribal error. And Yahya ibn ʿAwf: we have never found a biography of anyone by this name in the references available to us. As for the defect of the chain, it is "al-Furat ibn al-Sa'ib al-Jazari", who is very weak. Al-Bukhari said in al-Kabir 4/1/130: "They abandoned him, he is munkar al-hadith", and the imams likewise said of him. Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin (folio 187): he was one who narrated fabrications from the trustworthy, and brought mu'dal reports from the reliable; it is not permissible to argue with him, nor to narrate from him, nor to write his hadith except as a matter of testing. As for Maymun ibn Mihran, he is a well-known trustworthy Successor, a jurist and authority.
This report was transmitted by Ibn Kathir 1:50 without identification, with the wording "It was said: it is Islam". Al-Suyuti 1:15 transmitted it attributed to Ibn Jurayj only, with a typographical error in it: "Ibn Jurayj"!]]
And he also said:
Whenever a transgressor came with an evil intent, we hoped that it would be so for us.
So they turned back, obtaining nothing but disgrace, and the calamity destroyed them there.
I have never heard of men more vile than those who sought glory and violated Your sanctuary.
They dragged the hosts of their lands and the elephant, so that they might take your women captive.
[[The report 181 – Ibn al-Hanafiyyah: he is Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, and al-Hanafiyyah was his mother, Khawlah bint Jaʿfar from the Banu Hanifah; he became known by her ascription. The chain to him is weak: Muhammad ibn Rabiʿah al-Kilabi al-Ruʾasi: trustworthy, one of the teachers of Ahmad and Ibn Maʿin. Ismaʿil al-Azraq: he is Ismaʿil ibn Salman, and he is weak; Ibn Maʿin said: "his hadith is nothing", and Ibn Numayr and al-Nasa'i said: "abandoned"; Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin (p. 78, no. 35): "he alone narrates strange reports which he transmits from the well-known". Abu ʿUmar al-Bazzar: he is Dinar ibn ʿUmar al-Asadi al-Kufi, the blind, and he is trustworthy. The report was mentioned by Ibn Kathir 1:51 without attribution or chain.]]
Then ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib released the ring of the Kaʿbah's door, and he and those with him from Quraysh went up to the mountain peaks, where they took refuge, waiting to see what Abrahah would do to Makkah when he entered it. When Abrahah rose in the morning, he prepared to enter Makkah, readied his elephant, and arrayed his army; the elephant's name was Mahmud, and Abrahah was resolved to demolish the House and then return to Yemen. When they turned the elephant, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami came up, stood by its side, took hold of its ear and said: "Kneel down, Mahmud, and return safely whence you came, for you are in the sacred land of God." Then he released its ear, and the elephant knelt down. Nufayl ibn Habib ran off and climbed up the mountain. They struck the elephant to make it stand, but it refused; they struck it on the head with the tabarzin to make it stand, but it refused. They then thrust their hooks into its groin and goaded it to make it stand, but it refused. They turned it back toward Yemen, and it got up and trotted; they turned it toward Syria, and it did the same; they turned it toward the east, and it did the same; they turned it toward Makkah, and it knelt. God sent upon them birds from the sea, like swallows, each bird carrying three stones: a stone in its beak and two in its feet, like chickpeas and lentils. It did not strike any of them without their perishing, though not all of them were struck. They fled in haste along the road by which they had come, asking about Nufayl ibn Habib to guide them to the road to Yemen. Then Nufayl ibn Habib, when he saw what God had sent down upon them of His vengeance, said:
Where is the escape, when the Seeking God is the Pursuer? The one with the cleft lip is defeated, not the victor.
[[The report 182 – this is from the tafsir of al-Suddi, and its chain has been explained earlier: 168. Ibn Kathir 1:50 and al-Suyuti 1:15 transmitted it.]]
They fled, falling by every road and perishing at every watering place. Abrahah was struck in his body, and they carried him with them; his fingers fell off one by one, and each time a finger fell, it was followed by a discharge that dripped pus and blood, until they brought him to Sanaa, and he was like a young bird. He did not die until his chest split open from his heart, so they claim.
⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Yaʿqub ibn ʿUtbah ibn al-Mughirah ibn al-Akhnas, that he related that the first measles and smallpox were seen in the land of the Arabs that year, and that the first thing seen there was the bitter trees: the harmal, the colocynth, and the ʿushr, that year.
⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning his words: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ Abrahah al-Ashram came one day from Abyssinia, with those who were counted among the people of Yemen, to the House of God to demolish it, on account of a church they had which the Arabs had destroyed in the land of Yemen. They came with their elephant until, when they were at al-Saffah, it knelt down; whenever they turned it toward the House of God, it lay its neck on the ground, and whenever they turned it toward their own land, it went off at a trot. Until, when they were at Nakhlah al-Yamaniyyah, God sent upon them birds, white, in flocks. The ababil means many. With each bird were three stones: two in its feet and one in its beak. They kept striking them with them until God, mighty and majestic, made them like eaten chaff. He said: Abu Yaksum, who is Abrahah, escaped, and whenever he arrived in a land some of his flesh would fall off, until he reached his people, informed them of the news, and then died.
* *
As for His words: ﴿so He made them like eaten chaff﴾
That is, may He be exalted and remembered: God made the companions of the elephant like a crop that animals ate and then voided, so it dried up and its parts scattered. He likened the cutting apart of their limbs and the scattering of their body parts by the punishment that befell them to the scattering of the parts of the dung that results from eating the crop.
Some have said: al-ʿaṣf is the outer husk that surrounds the grain of wheat, like its covering.
Those who said that it refers to the leaves of the crop:
⁕ Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words: ﴿like eaten chaff﴾: he said: the leaves of wheat.
⁕ Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Mamar, from Qatadah: ﴿like eaten chaff﴾ he said: it is straw.
⁕ It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Muʿadh say: ʿUbayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say concerning His words ﴿like eaten chaff﴾: like eaten crops.
⁕ Muhammad ibn ʿAmarah al-Asadi narrated to me, saying: Zurayq ibn Marzuq narrated to us, saying: Hubayrah narrated to us, from Salamah ibn Nubayt, from al-Dahhak, concerning His words ﴿like eaten chaff﴾: he said: it is the hubur in Nabataean, and in another report: the maqhur (crushed).
⁕ Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words: ﴿So He made them like eaten chaff﴾: he said: the leaves of the crop and the leaves of herbs, when the beasts eat them and then void them, so they become dung.
Those who said that it refers to the husk of the grain:
⁕ Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿like eaten chaff﴾ he said: the wheat is eaten and its chaff is thrown away by the wind; al-ʿaṣf is what is above the wheat: it is the husk of the wheat.
Others said in this regard:
⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Sinan, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit: ﴿like eaten chaff﴾ he said: like food that has been eaten.
End of the tafsir of Surah al-Fil.

The interpretation of His words, exalted be His names: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plot go astray? And He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and He made them like eaten-up stalks.﴾

He, may His mention be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Have you not looked, O Muhammad, with the eye of your heart, so that you see by it ﴿how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant﴾, those who came from Yemen intending to destroy the Ka'bah, from Abyssinia, whose leader was Abrahah al-Habashi, the one with the cut nose, ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾

That is: Did He not make the effort of the Abyssinians, the companions of the elephant, in destroying the Ka'bah, ﴿go astray﴾, meaning: go astray from what they wanted and attempted of its destruction.

* *

As for His words: ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾

He, may His mention be exalted, says: And your Lord sent against them birds scattered, following one another from various directions. The word ﴿ababil﴾ (flocks) is a plural with no singular, like ash-shamatit and al-'abadid and the like. Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna claimed that he had not seen anyone assign a singular to it. Al-Farra' said: I have not heard from the Arabs anything regarding its singular. He said: Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi, who was trustworthy, claimed that he had heard that its singular is ﴿ibalah﴾ (إبالة). Al-Kisa'i used to say: I heard the grammarians say: ﴿ibul﴾ (إبول), like ﴿'ujul﴾ (عجول). He said: And I have heard some grammarians say: its singular is ﴿abil﴾ (أبيل).

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said something similar to what we have said about ﴿ababil﴾.

Those who said that:

• Sawwar ibn 'Abd Allah related to us, he said: Yahya ibn Sa'id related to us, he said: Hammad ibn Salamah related to us, from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, from Zirr, from 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: groups.

• Ibn Bashshar related to us, he said: Yahya and 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, both said: Hammad ibn Salamah related to us, from 'Asim, from Zirr, from 'Abd Allah, he said: the groups (al-firaq).

• 'Ali related to me, he said: Abu Salih related to us, he said: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: they follow one another.

• Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, he said: my father related to me, he said: my paternal uncle related to me, he said: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾, he said: they are those that follow one another.

• Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, he said: 'Abd al-A'la related to me, he said: Dawud related to us, from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal, that he said regarding ﴿birds in flocks﴾: they are herds (al-aqatee'), like camels gathered in groups (al-ibil al-mu'abbalah).

• Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Ya'qub al-Qummi related to us, from Ja'far, from Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza, ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: scattered.

• Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Waki' related to us, he said: al-Fadl related to us, from al-Hasan, ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: the many.

• Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Waki' related to us, from Isra'il, from Jabir, from Ibn Sabit, from Abu Salamah, the two said: ﴿al-ababil﴾ means the troops (al-zumar).

• Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, he said: Abu 'Asim related to us, he said: 'Isa related to us, and al-Harith related to me, he said: al-Hasan related to us, he said: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of God ﴿ababil﴾, he said: they are scattered, following one another, gathered together.

• Bishr related to us, he said: Yazid related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, he said: ﴿ababil﴾ means the many.

• Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, he said: ﴿ababil﴾ means the many.

• It has been related to me from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd related to us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾: he says: successive, one after another.

• Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾: ﴿ababil﴾ means the varied, coming from here and coming from there; they came to them from every place.

It has been mentioned that they were birds brought out from the sea. Some of them said: they came from the direction of the sea.

Then they differed regarding their description. Some of them said: they were white.

Others said: they were black.

Others said: they were green, with beaks like the beaks of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

• Ya'qub related to me, he said: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: Ibn 'Abbas said: they were birds, and they were birds with beaks like the beaks of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

• al-Hasan ibn Khalaf al-Wasiti related to me, he said: Waki' and Rawh ibn 'Ubadah related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from Ibn 'Abbas, the like of it.

• Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Waki' related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Ibn 'Abbas, something similar.

• Ya'qub related to us, he said: Hushaym related to us, he said: Husayn informed us, from 'Ikrimah, regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: they were birds that came out green, came out of the sea, with heads like the heads of beasts of prey.

• Ibn Bashshar related to us, he said: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, he said: Sufyan related to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: they are black birds of the sea, with stones in their beaks and talons.

• Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr: ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: black, of the sea, with stones in their talons and beaks.

• He said: Mihran related to us, from Kharijah, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: they had beaks like the beaks of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

• Yahya ibn Talhah al-Yarbu'i related to us, he said: Fudayl ibn 'Iyad related to us, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His words ﴿birds in flocks﴾, he said: green birds with yellow beaks, which moved among them.

• Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Waki' related to us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, he said: black birds carrying stones in their talons and beaks.

* *

As for His words: ﴿striking them with stones of hard clay﴾

He, may His mention be exalted, says: these birds, the ﴿ababil﴾ which God sent against the companions of the elephant, strike them with stones of ﴿sijjil﴾ (hard clay).

We have explained the meaning of ﴿sijjil﴾ in another place, but we will mention here some of what has been said about it, from the sayings of those whom we did not mention in that place.

Those who said that:

• Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from al-Suddi, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿stones of sijjil﴾, he said: clay in stones.

• al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Dhari' related to me, he said: Yazid ibn Zurayi' related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿striking them with stones of sijjil﴾, he said: of clay.

• Ibn Bashshar related to us, he said: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, he said: Sufyan related to us, from al-Suddi, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿stones of sijjil﴾, he said: sank wa-kul (Persian: stone and clay).

• al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Dhari' related to me, he said: Yazid ibn Zurayi' related to us, from 'Imarah ibn Abi Hafsah, from 'Ikrimah, regarding His words ﴿striking them with stones of sijjil﴾, he said: of clay.

• Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far related to us, he said: Shu'bah related to us, from Sharqi, he said: I heard 'Ikrimah say: ﴿striking them with stones of sijjil﴾, he said: sank wa-kul.

• Ya'qub related to me, he said: Hushaym related to us, he said: Husayn informed us, from 'Ikrimah, he said: They were striking them with stones, with which the smallpox (al-judari) came out upon whoever was struck. He said: That was the first day in which smallpox was seen; he said: it had not been seen before that day, nor after it.

• Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from Musa ibn Abi 'A'ishah, he said: Abu al-Kunud mentioned: smaller than a chickpea (al-himmasah) and larger than a lentil (al-'adasah).

• Ibn Bashshar related to us, he said: Abu Ahmad related to us, he said: Sufyan related to us, from Musa ibn Abi 'A'ishah, he said: the stones with which they were struck were larger than a lentil and smaller than a chickpea.

• He said: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri related to us, he said: Isra'il related to us, from Musa ibn Abi 'A'ishah, from 'Imran, the like of it.

• Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Waki' related to us, from Sufyan, from al-Suddi, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: sijjil in Persian: sank wa-kul, stone and clay.

• Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Waki' related to us, from Isra'il, from Jabir ibn Sabit, he said: it is in the foreign tongue: sank wa-kul.

• Bishr related to us, he said: Yazid related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, he said: With every bird were three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak, and it began striking them with them.

• Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿stones of sijjil﴾, he said: it is of clay.

• Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, he said: They were white birds that came out from the direction of the sea; with every bird were three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak, and it did not strike anything without crushing it.

• Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: 'Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Ya'qub informed us that his father informed him that it had reached him that the birds which struck with stones were carrying them in their mouths, and when they threw them, the skin blistered from them.

Others said: the meaning of that is: they strike them with stones from the lowest heaven.

Those who said that:

• Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿striking them with stones of sijjil﴾, he said: the lowest heaven, and he said: the lowest heaven is named sijjil, and it is the one from which God, may He be exalted and mighty, sent down (punishment) upon the people of Lut.

He said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: 'Amr ibn al-Harith informed us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal, that it had reached him that the birds which struck with stones were birds that come out of the sea, and that sijjil is the lowest heaven. And this saying that Ibn Zayd stated, we do not know any soundness for it in a report or in reason or in language, and the names of things are only known through a language in common use, or a report from God, may His mention be exalted.

The cause for which the punishment of God, may He be exalted, fell upon the companions of the elephant was the march of Abrahah al-Habashi with his army, with the elephant, toward the Sacred House of God to destroy it.

What prompted him to that was what:

• Ibn Humayd related it to us, he said: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us, he said: Ibn Ishaq related to us, that Abrahah built a church in San'a', and he was a Christian, and he named it al-Qulays; none like it had been seen in its time anywhere on earth. And he wrote to the Negus, king of Abyssinia: "Verily I have built for you, O king, a church, the like of which has not been built for any king before you, and I will not stop until I divert to it the pilgrims of the Arabs." [[Report 178 – this is a mawquf report on Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and its chain is sound: Mahmud ibn Khidash, with a kasra on the kha' and a fatha on the dal and a shin at the end, al-Talaqani: a trustworthy man of truthfulness, died on Wednesday, 14 Sha'ban 250, as in al-Tarikh al-Saghir of al-Bukhari: 247. Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Ru'asi: trustworthy, firm, intelligent; Ahmad and other memorizers related from him. Al-Hasan and 'Ali, the two sons of Salih ibn Salih ibn Hayy: both trustworthy, and they were twin brothers. Whoever spoke about al-Hasan spoke without proof, and we have authenticated him in al-Musnad: 2403, and his brother in it: 220. And 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Aqil ibn Abi Talib, and his mother Zaynab al-Sughra bint 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: a trustworthy Successor (tabi'i), and there is no proof for whoever spoke against him.

The report was transmitted by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:258–259, through the path of Abu Nu'aym from al-Hasan ibn Salih alone, with this chain. And he said: "This is a hadith with a sound chain, and the two (Bukhari and Muslim) did not narrate it." And al-Dhahabi agreed with him. And Ibn Kathir mentioned it, 1:50, and al-Suyuti 1:15, and al-Shawkani 1:13.]] When the Arabs spoke of Abrahah's letter to the Negus, a man from the Nasa'ah, one of Banu Faqim and then one of Banu Malik, became angry, so he went out until he came to al-Qulays, sat in it, then went out and joined his land. Abrahah was informed of that, and said: "Who did this?" It was said: "A man from the people of this House, which the Arabs make pilgrimage to in Mecca, who heard your words: 'I will divert to it the pilgrims of the Arabs,' so he became angry, and came and sat in it," meaning that it was not worthy of that. At that, Abrahah became furious, and swore that he would march upon the House and demolish it.

With Abrahah were men of the Arabs who had come to him seeking his favour, among them Muhammad ibn Khuza'i ibn Hizabah al-Dhakwani, then al-Sulami, along with a group of his people, and with him was a brother of his called Qays ibn Khuza'i. While they were with him, a servant of Abrahah came upon them, so he sent them his food, and he used to eat the testicles (al-khusa). When the people brought his food, they said: "By God, if we eat this, the Arabs will never cease to revile us with it as long as we live." So Muhammad ibn Khuza'i stood up, went to Abrahah and said: "O king, this is a day of festival for us, and we eat in it only the cheek-meat and the hands," and Abrahah said to him: "We will send to you whatever you wish, for I honoured you with my food, because of your standing with me."

Then Abrahah crowned Muhammad ibn Khuza'i and appointed him over Mudar, and ordered him to go among the people, calling them to pilgrimage to al-Qulayyis, his church which he built. Muhammad ibn Khuza'i set out until, when he alighted in some land of Banu Kinanah, and the people of Tihamah had learned of his affair and what he had come for, they sent to him a man from Hudhayl called 'Urwah ibn Hiyad al-Mula'i, who shot him with an arrow and killed him. Qays ibn Khuza'i, Muhammad's brother, was with him, and he fled when his brother was killed, and joined Abrahah and informed him of the killing. That increased Abrahah's anger and rage, and he swore that he would certainly raid Banu Kinanah and certainly demolish the House.

Then when Abrahah resolved to march toward the House, he ordered the Habashan (the Abyssinian troops) to prepare and equip themselves, and he went out with the elephant. The Arabs heard of that, and they regarded it as grave and were horrified by it, and they saw that fighting him was an obligation upon them, when they heard that he intended to demolish the Ka'bah, the Sacred House of God. A man who was among the nobles and kings of Yemen, called Dhu Nafr, went out, and called his people and those among the rest of the Arabs who answered him, to fight Abrahah and to strive against him for the House of God, and against what he intended of its demolition and ruin. Those who answered him answered, and he confronted him and fought him, and he was defeated and his companions scattered, and Dhu Nafr was taken prisoner. When Abrahah wished to kill him, Dhu Nafr said: "O king, do not kill me, for perhaps my remaining with you will be better for you than my killing." So he spared him from death, and held him in bonds with himself. Abrahah was a forbearing man.

Then Abrahah proceeded on that course of his, aiming at what he had set out for, until, when he was in the land of Khath'am, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami confronted him, with the two Khath'am clans, Shahran and Nahis, and those with him from the Arab tribes. He fought him, and Abrahah defeated him and took him prisoner, and he was brought to him. When he resolved to kill him, Nufayl said to him: "O king, do not kill me, for I am your guide in the land of the Arabs, and these two hands of mine are yours over my clans, Shahran and Nahis, with hearing and obedience." So he pardoned him and released him, and he went out with him, guiding him on the road. When he passed by al-Ta'if, Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib went out to him with men of Thaqif, and said: "O king, we are only your slaves, listening to you and obeying you; there is no opposition from us to you, and this house of ours is not the house you seek" — meaning al-Lat — "you only seek the house that is in Mecca" — meaning the Ka'bah — "and we will send with you someone to guide you." So he overlooked them, and they sent with him Abu Righal. Abrahah set out, and Abu Righal was with him, until he brought him down at al-Mughammas. When he had brought him down there, Abu Righal died there, and the Arabs stoned his grave, and it is the grave which people stone at al-Mughammas.

When Abrahah alighted at al-Mughammas, he sent a man from the Abyssinians, called al-Aswad ibn Maqsud, with horses of his, until he reached Mecca, and he drove to him the property of the people of Mecca from Quraysh and others, and he seized two hundred camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, who at that time was the chief and lord of Quraysh. Quraysh, Kinanah, Hudhayl, and whoever was with them in the Sanctuary of the people resolved to fight him, then they realized they had no power against him, so they abandoned that. Abrahah sent Hunatah al-Himyari to Mecca and said to him: "Ask about the lord of this city and its nobleman, then say to him: The king says to you: I have not come to fight you; I have only come to demolish the House. If you do not stand in its way with war, I have no need for your blood. If he does not wish to fight me, then bring him to me."

When Hunatah entered Makkah, he asked about the leader and noblest of Quraysh, and was told: ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hashim ibn ʿAbd Manaf ibn Qusayy. So he came to him and told him what Abrahah had ordered. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said: "By God, we do not intend to fight him, nor do we have the strength for that. This is the Sacred House of God, and the house of His friend Abraham, peace be upon him—or as he said. If He protects it, it is His house and His sanctuary; and if He leaves it between Abrahah and it, by God, we have no one to defend it against him—or as he said." Hunatah said to him: "Then come with me to the king, for he has ordered me to bring you to him." So ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib set out with him, accompanied by some of his sons, until they reached the army. He asked about Dhu Nafar, who was a friend of his, and was directed to him. He came to him while he was in his confinement and said: "O Dhu Nafar, do you have any means of help regarding what has befallen us?" Dhu Nafar, who was his friend, replied: "What help can a man have who is a captive in the hand of a king, awaiting to be killed morning or evening! I have no help in anything that has befallen you, except that Unays, the driver of the elephant, is a friend of mine. I will send for him and charge him with you, and impress upon him the magnitude of your right, and ask him to seek permission for you to see the king, so you may speak to him about what you want, and he may intercede for you with him for good, if he is able to do so." He said: "That is enough for me." So Dhu Nafar sent to Unays, and he came, and Dhu Nafar said: "O Unays, ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib is the leader of Quraysh and the owner of the caravans of Makkah; he feeds people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain tops, and the king has taken from him two hundred camels. So seek permission for him to see him, and plead his cause with him as much as you can." He said: "I will do so."
Unays spoke to Abrahah, saying: "O King, this is the leader of Quraysh at your gate, seeking permission to see you, and he is the owner of the caravans of Makkah, who feeds people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain tops. So grant him permission to see you, that he may speak to you about his need, and be kind to him." He said: Abrahah granted him permission. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was an imposing, handsome, and large man. When Abrahah saw him, he was struck with awe of him and honored him, and disliked that the Abyssinians should see him sit beneath him, so Abrahah got down from his throne and sat on his carpet, and made him sit beside him on it. Then he said to his interpreter: "Ask him what his need of the king is." The interpreter said that to him, and ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said: "My need of the king is that he return to me my two hundred camels which he has taken from me." When he said that, Abrahah said to his interpreter: "Tell him: I was impressed by you when I saw you, but I lost interest in you when you spoke to me. Do you speak to me about two hundred camels that I have taken from you, and leave aside a house which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, which I have come to demolish, and not speak to me about it?" ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said to him: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." He said: "He will not prevent me." He said: "Then that is your affair; return my camels to me."
It was said by some scholars that Yamur ibn Nufathah ibn ʿAdi ibn al-Dil ibn Bakr ibn ʿAbd Manaf ibn Kinanah, who was then the leader of the Banu Kinanah, went with ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib to Abrahah when Hunatah had sent for him, as did Khuwaylid ibn Wathilah al-Hudhali, who was then the leader of Hudhayl. They offered Abrahah a third of the wealth of Tihamah on condition that he would turn back from them and not demolish the House, but he refused, and God knows best.
Abrahah had returned to ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib the camels that had been taken for him. When they left him, ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib went back to Quraysh and informed them of the news, and ordered them to leave Makkah and take refuge in the mountain peaks and the ravines, fearing for them the harm of the army. Then ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib stood, took hold of the ring of the door of the Kaʿbah, and with him stood a group of Quraysh, supplicating God and seeking His aid against Abrahah and his troops. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, while holding the ring of the Kaʿbah's door, said:
O Lord, I do not hope for them other than You; O Lord, protect from them Your sanctuary.
Surely the enemy of the House is he who is hostile to You; prevent them from ruining Your dwelling.
[[The narration 179 – its chain is weak, as its weakness was explained earlier: 137. This wording was transmitted by Ibn Kathir 1:50 without chain or attribution. Al-Suyuti 1:14 transmitted it in abridged form and attributed it to al-Tabari only.]]
And he also said:
O God, indeed a man defends his camp; so defend Your sanctuary.
Let not their cross and their stratagem prevail against Your stratagem tomorrow.
If You do so, then perhaps You will have a purpose that You have in mind.
And if You do so, it is a matter by which You complete Your deed.
[[The report 180 – its chain is very weak, despite our ignorance of the state of some of its narrators: Musa ibn Sahl al-Razi, Tabari's teacher: we have not determined which man he is; perhaps he is "Musa ibn Sahl ibn Qadim, also said Ibn Musa Abu ʿUmar al-Ramli, originally from Nasa". He is a teacher of al-Tabari recorded in al-Tahdhib 10:347, but he is not described as "al-Razi". In the manuscript it was written: "Sahl ibn Musa"! We have not found this biography either, and we think it is a scribal error. And Yahya ibn ʿAwf: we have never found a biography of anyone by this name in the references available to us. As for the defect of the chain, it is "al-Furat ibn al-Sa'ib al-Jazari", who is very weak. Al-Bukhari said in al-Kabir 4/1/130: "They abandoned him, he is munkar al-hadith", and the imams likewise said of him. Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin (folio 187): he was one who narrated fabrications from the trustworthy, and brought mu'dal reports from the reliable; it is not permissible to argue with him, nor to narrate from him, nor to write his hadith except as a matter of testing. As for Maymun ibn Mihran, he is a well-known trustworthy Successor, a jurist and authority.
This report was transmitted by Ibn Kathir 1:50 without identification, with the wording "It was said: it is Islam". Al-Suyuti 1:15 transmitted it attributed to Ibn Jurayj only, with a typographical error in it: "Ibn Jurayj"!]]
And he also said:
Whenever a transgressor came with an evil intent, we hoped that it would be so for us.
So they turned back, obtaining nothing but disgrace, and the calamity destroyed them there.
I have never heard of men more vile than those who sought glory and violated Your sanctuary.
They dragged the hosts of their lands and the elephant, so that they might take your women captive.
[[The report 181 – Ibn al-Hanafiyyah: he is Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, and al-Hanafiyyah was his mother, Khawlah bint Jaʿfar from the Banu Hanifah; he became known by her ascription. The chain to him is weak: Muhammad ibn Rabiʿah al-Kilabi al-Ruʾasi: trustworthy, one of the teachers of Ahmad and Ibn Maʿin. Ismaʿil al-Azraq: he is Ismaʿil ibn Salman, and he is weak; Ibn Maʿin said: "his hadith is nothing", and Ibn Numayr and al-Nasa'i said: "abandoned"; Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin (p. 78, no. 35): "he alone narrates strange reports which he transmits from the well-known". Abu ʿUmar al-Bazzar: he is Dinar ibn ʿUmar al-Asadi al-Kufi, the blind, and he is trustworthy. The report was mentioned by Ibn Kathir 1:51 without attribution or chain.]]
Then ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib released the ring of the Kaʿbah's door, and he and those with him from Quraysh went up to the mountain peaks, where they took refuge, waiting to see what Abrahah would do to Makkah when he entered it. When Abrahah rose in the morning, he prepared to enter Makkah, readied his elephant, and arrayed his army; the elephant's name was Mahmud, and Abrahah was resolved to demolish the House and then return to Yemen. When they turned the elephant, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami came up, stood by its side, took hold of its ear and said: "Kneel down, Mahmud, and return safely whence you came, for you are in the sacred land of God." Then he released its ear, and the elephant knelt down. Nufayl ibn Habib ran off and climbed up the mountain. They struck the elephant to make it stand, but it refused; they struck it on the head with the tabarzin to make it stand, but it refused. They then thrust their hooks into its groin and goaded it to make it stand, but it refused. They turned it back toward Yemen, and it got up and trotted; they turned it toward Syria, and it did the same; they turned it toward the east, and it did the same; they turned it toward Makkah, and it knelt. God sent upon them birds from the sea, like swallows, each bird carrying three stones: a stone in its beak and two in its feet, like chickpeas and lentils. It did not strike any of them without their perishing, though not all of them were struck. They fled in haste along the road by which they had come, asking about Nufayl ibn Habib to guide them to the road to Yemen. Then Nufayl ibn Habib, when he saw what God had sent down upon them of His vengeance, said:
Where is the escape, when the Seeking God is the Pursuer? The one with the cleft lip is defeated, not the victor.
[[The report 182 – this is from the tafsir of al-Suddi, and its chain has been explained earlier: 168. Ibn Kathir 1:50 and al-Suyuti 1:15 transmitted it.]]
They fled, falling by every road and perishing at every watering place. Abrahah was struck in his body, and they carried him with them; his fingers fell off one by one, and each time a finger fell, it was followed by a discharge that dripped pus and blood, until they brought him to Sanaa, and he was like a young bird. He did not die until his chest split open from his heart, so they claim.
⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Yaʿqub ibn ʿUtbah ibn al-Mughirah ibn al-Akhnas, that he related that the first measles and smallpox were seen in the land of the Arabs that year, and that the first thing seen there was the bitter trees: the harmal, the colocynth, and the ʿushr, that year.
⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning his words: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ Abrahah al-Ashram came one day from Abyssinia, with those who were counted among the people of Yemen, to the House of God to demolish it, on account of a church they had which the Arabs had destroyed in the land of Yemen. They came with their elephant until, when they were at al-Saffah, it knelt down; whenever they turned it toward the House of God, it lay its neck on the ground, and whenever they turned it toward their own land, it went off at a trot. Until, when they were at Nakhlah al-Yamaniyyah, God sent upon them birds, white, in flocks. The ababil means many. With each bird were three stones: two in its feet and one in its beak. They kept striking them with them until God, mighty and majestic, made them like eaten chaff. He said: Abu Yaksum, who is Abrahah, escaped, and whenever he arrived in a land some of his flesh would fall off, until he reached his people, informed them of the news, and then died.
* *
As for His words: ﴿so He made them like eaten chaff﴾
That is, may He be exalted and remembered: God made the companions of the elephant like a crop that animals ate and then voided, so it dried up and its parts scattered. He likened the cutting apart of their limbs and the scattering of their body parts by the punishment that befell them to the scattering of the parts of the dung that results from eating the crop.
Some have said: al-ʿaṣf is the outer husk that surrounds the grain of wheat, like its covering.
Those who said that it refers to the leaves of the crop:
⁕ Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words: ﴿like eaten chaff﴾: he said: the leaves of wheat.
⁕ Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Mamar, from Qatadah: ﴿like eaten chaff﴾ he said: it is straw.
⁕ It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Muʿadh say: ʿUbayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say concerning His words ﴿like eaten chaff﴾: like eaten crops.
⁕ Muhammad ibn ʿAmarah al-Asadi narrated to me, saying: Zurayq ibn Marzuq narrated to us, saying: Hubayrah narrated to us, from Salamah ibn Nubayt, from al-Dahhak, concerning His words ﴿like eaten chaff﴾: he said: it is the hubur in Nabataean, and in another report: the maqhur (crushed).
⁕ Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words: ﴿So He made them like eaten chaff﴾: he said: the leaves of the crop and the leaves of herbs, when the beasts eat them and then void them, so they become dung.
Those who said that it refers to the husk of the grain:
⁕ Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿like eaten chaff﴾ he said: the wheat is eaten and its chaff is thrown away by the wind; al-ʿaṣf is what is above the wheat: it is the husk of the wheat.
Others said in this regard:
⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Sinan, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit: ﴿like eaten chaff﴾ he said: like food that has been eaten.
End of the tafsir of Surah al-Fil.
